newsitem.title: UK: World says Bhutto ousting internal affair.
newsitem.headline: World says Bhutto ousting internal affair.

text.p: Britain, India and the Commonwealth on Tuesday delivered identical messages after the ousting of Pakistani Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto -- her dismissal was an internal affair and not their concern.
Even though the military has ruled Pakistan for 24 of its 49 years as an independent state, analysts did not expect them to take over again.

"They would find it very difficult to control the country themselves and it would be like being handed a poisoned chalice," said Terry Taylor, assistant director of the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies.
Britain, former colonial masters of Pakistan, took several hours to make any comment at all and then it was muted.
"This is entirely a matter for Pakistan and we have no comment to make. We shall of course deal normally with the caretaker government of Meraj Khalid," a Foreign Office spokesman said.
The Commonwealth, which mainly groups Britain's former colonies and protectorates, also adopted a "hands-off" approach.
A spokesman for the Commonwealth secretariat said: "This is strictly an internal matter for Pakistan. It is not something the Commonwealth will get involved in unless it was asked to."
Indian Prime Minister H.D.Deve Gowda echoed this sentiment, saying in Harare: "We see these events as Pakistan's internal developments and are following them closely."
India has fought three wars with Pakistan over the past half century. Japan, Pakistan's main aid donor, said it would not affect relations between Tokyo and Islamabad.
Bhutto was sacked on Tuesday for the second time in her political career as President Farooq Leghari accused her government of corruption, nepotism and misrule.
He ordered elections for February 3 and named veteran politician Khalid as caretaker prime minister. Troops moved into the capital Islamabad in the early hours to guard key installations.
Britain's opposition Labour Party, whose foreign affairs spokesman Robin Cook is visiting Islamabad, said international pressure should be applied to ensure elections are held next February.
Labour's Robin Cook, speaking from Islamabad, said: "The world community must hold the new caretaker government to its undertaking that elections will be held on February 3."
He said the country faced serious problems paying its way because its defence budget takes a third of public spending.

"An equal priority must be restoration of human rights, especially in Karachi where, according to the president, thousands of people have been killed by police action in the last three years," he said.

The military has maintained a low profile in the latest crisis to hit Pakistan but President Leghari would have been unlikely to act without the approval and co-operation of the generals, analysts said.

"I think a military takeover is not on the cards," Taylor said. "The problem is how the opposition party supporters will react in physical terms. It will take three or four days to see if there will be a violent reaction," he added.
